insights.text: The expected growth rate $\mu$ of the stock drops out of the price. A portfolio of one option and $\Delta = \partial V / \partial S$ shares sold short has no $dW$ term left, so it is riskless and must earn the risk-free rate $r$, and nothing in that argument depends on $\mu$.

Volatility enters through the curvature term $\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}$, which is what the hedged position gains as the stock moves. The more the stock moves, the more that curvature is worth.

The equation alone has many solutions. The one that prices an option is picked out by its value on the expiration date, which for a call is

$$V = \max(S - K, 0)$$

and for a put $\max(K - S, 0)$.

Each assumption is a simplification: no dividends, a constant $\sigma$ and $r$, trading that is continuous and costs nothing, no risk-free profit, and exercise only at expiration. Real markets break most of them, and the extensions of the model relax them one at a time.

Put–call parity, $C - P = S - K e^{-rT}$, has no $\sigma$ in it and holds whatever model drives the stock, so it checks any pair of quoted prices. The call and the put also share $d_1$ and $d_2$, so one calculation prices both.

takeaways: The stock follows $dS = \mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW$, so its price can never become negative.
Holding the option and selling $\Delta = \partial V / \partial S$ shares removes the random part over a short time.
A riskless portfolio must earn the risk-free rate $r$, and setting its change equal to $r \Pi\, dt$ gives the Black–Scholes equation.
The price of an option does not depend on how fast the stock is expected to rise.
A call bought and a put sold at the same strike and expiration are worth $S - K e^{-rT}$.
cheat-sheet:
### Assumptions

- No dividends during the life of the option.
- The volatility $\sigma$ and the rate $r$ are constants.
- Trading is continuous and costs nothing, and short sales of any size are allowed.
- No risk-free profit can be made.
- The option is European: it is exercised only at expiration.

### The equation

$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} + r S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} - r V = 0$$

### The prices

$$C = S\,N(d_1) - K e^{-rT} N(d_2)$$

$$P = K e^{-rT} N(-d_2) - S\,N(-d_1)$$

$$d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + \left(r + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| $S$ | the stock price now |
| $K$ | the strike |
| $r$ | the risk-free rate |
| $\sigma$ | the volatility |
| $T$ | the time left until expiration |
| $N$ | the distribution function of the standard normal |

### Rules of thumb

- The price of an option does not depend on the expected growth rate $\mu$.
- $C - P = S - K e^{-rT}$ under any model of the stock.
- One calculation of $d_1$ and $d_2$ prices both options.
